syntax_features.boundary: This value does not project into worksheet spill cells; grid placement, blockers, A1# and implicit intersection remain catalogued only.

syntax_features.definition: Six scalar comparison operators with explicit number < text < Boolean ranking, counterpart-typed blank adaptation, left error propagation and finite binary64 numeric comparisons. ASCII text is case-insensitive; non-ASCII uses an explicit exact UTF-8 ordinal local profile.
syntax_features.boundary: Excel-targeted type/blank cases remain unobserved; primary operator/precedence documentation and compatible MATCH ordering do not establish every coercion/collation case. Native primitives retain their separate legacy comparison contract.

semantics.stage3_scalar_profile: Classic scalar Excel errors and transported #CALC!/#SPILL! values trigger lazy fallback; blank selected inputs/fallbacks become empty text. Implementation diagnostics and Rust Unsupported/Parse failures are not Excel errors. Modern error interception is a local unobserved profile; no spill placement implied.

semantics.selected_reference_profile: A one-cell reference that IF, IFERROR, IFNA, IFS, SWITCH, CHOOSE or XLOOKUP selects, and the cell that INDEX returns from a range, is still a reference when SUM receives it. Text and logical values in that cell are ignored, as they are for the same cell named directly, so with A1 = TRUE both SUM(A1) and SUM(IF(TRUE,A1)) are 0. A value typed directly and selected the same way is still a typed value, so SUM(IF(TRUE,TRUE)) is 1 and SUM(IF(TRUE,"5")) is 5. Microsoft's page Use the SUM function to sum numbers in a range gives =SUM("5", 15, TRUE) = 21 with "The text value \"5\" is first translated into a number, and the logical value TRUE is first translated into the number 1." and =SUM(A5,A6, 2) = 2 because "non-numeric values in references are not translated" and "the values in those cells are ignored". Microsoft's CHOOSE page says of SUM(CHOOSE(2,A1:A10,B1:B10,C1:C10)): "The CHOOSE function is evaluated first, returning the reference B1:B10." No Microsoft sentence says what SUM does with a one-cell reference selected by IF or the other functions. Treating it as a reference is a Workbook Forge profile, the same rule this evaluator already applied to COUNT, AND and OR, and it has not been checked in Excel. IFERROR still returns empty text, a typed value, when the selected cell is empty. INDEX is a reference here only when its first argument is a range. The Rust evaluator's INDEX also accepts a typed value or one cell as its first argument, and directly inside SUM that result is read as it was before this profile, so SUM(INDEX(TRUE,1)) is 1 there; the Python evaluator's INDEX returns #VALUE! for it. Behind IF or another selecting function the Rust evaluator still reads such an INDEX result as a reference, so SUM(IF(TRUE,INDEX(TRUE,1))) is 0 there.

coverage.note: The Microsoft function inventory contains 521 entries. One hundred seventy-one functions are conformance-tested with shared Python/Rust fixtures; the remaining 350 of the 521 inventoried functions are catalog-only. Criteria functions implement scalar criteria, comparison operators, case-insensitive text, wildcard escapes, and bounded range shapes. SUMIF and AVERAGEIF reject differently sized sum/average ranges even though Excel aligns those ranges from their top-left cell; that compatibility gap is explicit in semantic_specs. MINIFS and MAXIFS require matching range shapes, allow one required plus up to 126 additional criteria pairs, and return 0 when no numeric result matches. XLOOKUP and XMATCH support exact match_mode=0 with forward/reverse search_mode=1/-1 only; approximate, wildcard, binary, and array-spill results are unsupported. TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER support scalar delimiter extraction, optional arguments, negative instance numbers, match_end, and lazy if_not_found; their Excel locale collation and supplementary-plane character behavior remain unverified. ISNA, ISERR, ISERROR, and NA cover scalar inspection and creation of supported Excel error values; array error predicates and unsupported-syntax conversions remain out of scope. INT, TRUNC, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, MOD, and QUOTIENT add scalar directed rounding, floor/truncation, remainder, and integer-quotient behavior. Fractional num_digits values are truncated toward zero as an implementation rule; Microsoft pages do not specify this case, and direct Excel spot-checks remain outstanding. MONTH, DAYS, EDATE, and EOMONTH use the 1900 serial system and preserve its serial-60 compatibility date; DAYS subtracts numeric serials including their fractional parts. EDATE and EOMONTH truncate fractional month counts toward zero; both month-shift functions return whole-day serials, and EDATE discards a start serial's time fraction as an implementation profile rule. Locale-dependent text-date parsing and workbook-specific 1904 date systems are not modeled; time-fraction handling for EDATE/EOMONTH has not been spot-checked in Excel. HOUR, MINUTE, and SECOND extract whole-second components from numeric 1900-system serials; the serial ceiling and negative/non-finite input errors are evaluator profile rules not stated on the function pages. Locale-dependent time text such as '6:45 PM' is documented by Microsoft but not parsed here. The shared serial-to-seconds precision correction and TIME fractional-component truncation are evaluator profile rules that need Excel spot-checks. TIME accepts components from 0 through 32767, normalizes overflow, and returns a fraction of a day. IFS and SWITCH use ordered short-circuit evaluation and first-match selection; selected results may preserve a rectangular array through evaluate_result, but are not projected into worksheet cells. SWITCH treats ASCII text as case-insensitive and non-ASCII text as exact, with no cross-type coercion or locale collation. Microsoft documents selection/default behavior but not all evaluation and comparison details; these evaluator profile rules need a direct Excel spot-check. WEEKDAY, WEEKNUM, and ISOWEEKNUM add numeric 1900-system date serials, documented return selectors, System 1 and ISO week rules, and time-fraction flooring. Fractional return_type coercion and exact 1900 serial-60 week behavior are evaluator-profile rules that still need Excel spot-checks. WORKDAY and NETWORKDAYS use a Saturday/Sunday business calendar and scalar or cell-range holidays. NETWORKDAYS counts weekday endpoints inclusively; reversed-range sign, fractional date serials, holiday-cell coercion, serial 0, and serial 60 are explicit evaluator profiles that still need direct Excel spot-checks. WORKDAY truncates noninteger day offsets as Microsoft documents; holiday-cell coercion remains unverified. WORKDAY.INTL and NETWORKDAYS.INTL share numeric weekend codes, Monday-first seven-character masks, and range-based holiday handling. NETWORKDAYS.INTL documents inclusive and reversed-range counts plus zero for an all-one weekend mask. Its last example prose says 22 while the result column says 20 for mask 0010001 with holidays; fixtures follow the result column; WORKDAY.INTL documents zero-offset behavior and rejects the all-one mask, but its exact error is unspecified. Numeric selector coercion, date fractions, serial boundaries, and holiday-cell coercion remain profiles; holiday array constants and locale-sensitive date text are not implemented. DAYS360 and YEARFRAC add a bounded 30/360 and year-fraction slice. The published DAYS360 rules cover US NASD and European methods and negative direction; non-month-end US endpoint wording, numeric and blank-cell method handling, optional-slot parsing, fractional date serials, and serial 60 remain evaluator profiles. YEARFRAC covers bases 0-4, documented integer truncation and error codes, and Microsoft examples. Basis 1 uses a year-segmented Actual/Actual profile and reversed dates use a signed result; Microsoft does not specify those details on its function page, so neither is claimed as verified Excel behavior. The 1900 date system and serial 60 remain explicit evaluator profiles. The six COUP schedule formulas share a maturity-anchored, backward-stepped date schedule in the evaluator and expose separate function-specific outputs. Microsoft documents argument truncation, valid frequencies 1/2/4, basis values 0-4, output definitions, and date/frequency/basis/order errors. The maturity-anchored schedule, period/count equality behavior outside the documented strict COUPNCD/COUPPCD boundaries, basis-specific day counts, serial-60 behavior, and pre-zero internal coupon dates remain evaluator profiles. COUPDAYS basis 1 uses actual adjacent coupon-date serial difference but has not been checked against Excel; ExcelFinancialFunctions compatibility notes identify leap-year COUPDAYS differences, so shared expected values are not treated as Excel oracles. FV, PV, and PMT add a scalar periodic-cash-flow slice with shared sign, timing, zero-rate, omission, and numeric-profile cases. NPER inverts the periodic cash-flow equation, preserves negative and fractional results, and checks zero-rate and logarithm-domain boundaries under explicit evaluator profiles. Exact internal precision and undocumented input errors remain unverified. IPMT and PPMT split PMT into period interest and principal components; PPMT is defined as PMT minus IPMT, and both use explicit timing, range, numeric, and error profiles pending direct Excel checks. Function batch 1 (2026-11-12) adds 48 functions with 874 shared cases: scalar math and logical constants (SQRT, POWER, EXP, LN, LOG, LOG10, PI, SIGN, CEILING, FLOOR, CEILING.MATH, FLOOR.MATH, MROUND, TRUE, FALSE, XOR), range statistics (PRODUCT, SUMSQ, SUMPRODUCT, MEDIAN, LARGE, SMALL, RANK.EQ, RANK, STDEV.S, STDEV.P, VAR.S, VAR.P, AVERAGEA, MODE.SNGL), text, selection and dimensions (CONCATENATE, EXACT, PROPER, REPT, REPLACE, VALUE, CHAR, CODE, CHOOSE, HLOOKUP, ROWS, COLUMNS), and cash-flow finance (NPV, IRR, XNPV, XIRR, RATE, MIRR). A review of the batch on the same day added 24 of those cases, all but one of them profiles, corrected Rust so that an error value given as ref to RANK or RANK.EQ is returned as in Python, and recorded further departures from Microsoft's pages in semantic_specs: the FLOOR.MATH page's two sentences on mode disagree, CEILING.MATH's printed number range is not applied, RANK accepts a computed array, XNPV accepts a payment on the first date, and NPV counts directly typed logical values and numeric text. POWER(0,0)=1 and POWER(0,-1)=#NUM! follow the ^ operator; third-party reports that Excel returns #NUM! and #DIV/0! are recorded and were not observed in Excel by this project. No direct Excel Desktop checks were run. No source code was copied and no runtime dependency was added.

semantics.definition: Returns prorated accounting-period depreciation using a life-dependent coefficient under the French depreciation method. Microsoft currently marks the function deprecated and retained for old-workbook compatibility.
semantics.day_count_basis: Microsoft documents basis 0 or omitted as US/NASD 30/360, 1 as actual, 3 as actual/365, and 4 as European 30/360. Excel truncates basis to an integer and Office uses only 0, 1, 3, or 4; basis 2 is excluded.
semantics.coefficient_profile: Microsoft lists coefficient 1.5 for useful lives between 3 and 4, 2 for 5 and 6, and 2.5 above 6. The evaluator uses ceil(1/rate) before coefficient selection, following ExcelFinancialFunctions. It rejects raw useful lives <=3 and 4<=life<=5 as an evaluator profile resolving ambiguous overlapping Microsoft ranges; Apache OpenOffice uses different band selection and is retained as a comparison only.
semantics.equation_profile: Evaluator profile informed by ExcelFinancialFunctions: multiply rate by the life coefficient; prorate period 0 using the selected day-count fraction and round to whole currency units. When the original unrounded stub is exactly zero, substitute cost times the effective rate for period 0 and keep the base life. A positive stub adds one schedule step. Later periods use the remaining book value and the effective declining rate, switching to half of remaining book value when two schedule steps remain and to the full remaining book value on the following step. Period inputs after ceil(1/rate) still return zero. If book value is already below salvage, the later-period amount is zero. The calculation does not clamp every amount to remaining book value minus salvage, so a rounded step can carry the book value below salvage. These are reference-derived evaluator behaviors, not a general Microsoft-published equation or an Excel-verified claim.
semantics.period_index_profile: Evaluator profile: period 0 is the prorated stub and period 1 is the first post-stub depreciation amount. Microsoft documents a period-1 example of 776 but does not define the complete index schedule.
semantics.date_profile: Dates are numeric 1900-system Excel serials; fractional serials truncate toward zero to calendar days, locale text dates are unsupported, and purchase must precede first_period. Day-count leap-day handling follows the local serial calendar; exact Excel behavior remains unverified. Basis 1 uses denominator 366 only when the inclusive serial interval contains February 29, otherwise 365; serial 60 is treated as the shared 1900-system compatibility date 1900-02-29.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<cost, rate positive and finite, and period truncates toward zero to 0..100000. Useful-life and period ceilings, allowed basis values, date bounds/order, and error codes are evaluator profiles where Excel is silent or ambiguous.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions documents an Excel-compatible rounding switch for an edge case whose outputs differ by one unit; its ordinary path and Apache OpenOffice also differ in coefficient bands/validation. The evaluator uses half-up period rounding, the ceil-life coefficient profile, and the zero-stub full-year fallback. Shared cases include Microsoft’s displayed 776 example plus independent derivations/reference-derived cases; they do not establish Excel compatibility. No code is copied.

derived_examples.basis: 134/365 stub fraction times cost 2400 and effective 37.5% rate, rounded half-up because the interval contains no February 29; implementation-derived, not a Microsoft-published result.
A 3.5-year raw life selects coefficient 1.5; the full-period basis-3 stub is 1000*(2/7)*1.5, rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
A 5.5-year raw life selects coefficient 2; the full-period basis-3 stub is rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
A 6.5-year raw life selects coefficient 2.5; the full-period basis-3 stub is rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
The local NASD 30/360 helper yields 183/360 days; applying the 37.5% effective rate and half-up rounding. Reference/profile-derived, not Excel-checked.
The NASD 30/360 stub is zero, so the reference-derived evaluator profile uses cost*(2/7)*1.5 for period 0; half-up rounding gives 429. Not a Microsoft-published result.

semantics.rounding_profile: The period-0 amount and later period amounts are rounded half-up to whole currency units. If the prorated stub is exactly zero, the reference-derived evaluator profile substitutes the full-year effective-rate amount for period 0 and keeps the base life; a positive unrounded stub adds one schedule step. Because later amounts are not clamped to remaining book value minus salvage, cumulative depreciation can cross below salvage; subsequent periods return zero once book value is below salvage. This profile is informed by ExcelFinancialFunctions and is not directly checked against Excel.

semantics.definition: Returns depreciation for an accounting period under the French linear depreciation method, including prorated depreciation for an asset purchased during an accounting period.
semantics.day_count_basis: Microsoft documents basis 0 or omitted as US/NASD 30/360, 1 as actual, 3 as actual/365, and 4 as European 30/360. The Microsoft Excel Open Specification says Excel truncates basis to an integer and uses only 0, 1, 3, or 4; basis 2 is not used by Office. For basis 1, the evaluator uses 366 only when the inclusive serial interval contains February 29 (including compatibility serial 60); otherwise it uses 365.
semantics.equation_profile: Evaluator profile informed by the Apache-2.0 ExcelFinancialFunctions reference: period 0 normally returns min(cost*rate*stub_year_fraction, cost-salvage); when the unrounded stub is exactly zero, it substitutes min(cost*rate, cost-salvage). Later periods return min(cost*rate, remaining depreciable basis after period 0 and prior full annual amounts). The Excel function page does not publish a general equation.
semantics.period_index_profile: Evaluator profile: period 0 represents the prorated stub, period 1 is the first full annual amount. Microsoft documents a period-1 result of 360 for its 2400 cost and 15% rate example but does not define general period indexing; the reference implementation uses this zero-based stub convention.
semantics.date_profile: Dates are numeric 1900-system Excel serials; fractional serials are truncated toward zero to calendar days, text-date parsing is unsupported, and the purchase date must precede the first-period date. The date range and purchase-order restriction are evaluator profiles. Basis 1 uses a 366-day denominator only when the inclusive interval contains February 29; otherwise its denominator is 365. Serial 60 is treated as the shared 1900-system compatibility date 1900-02-29.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<cost, rate must be positive and finite, and period truncates toward zero to an integer from 0 through 100000. The reciprocal rate must be finite and its ceiling must not exceed 9,007,199,254,740,991. Domain bounds, period truncation/cap, date handling, and error codes are evaluator profiles where Microsoft is silent.
semantics.rounding_profile: AMORLINC retains fractional currency amounts; no per-period whole-unit rounding is applied by this evaluator. This is an evaluator profile, not a direct Excel check.
semantics.source_example_issue: The Microsoft Excel page data table puts the rate in A7 and basis 1 in A8, but the displayed formula passes A7 as both rate and basis. The Microsoft Open Specification says basis is truncated, so 0.15 selects basis 0, not the stated Actual basis 1. The separate DAX example uses a literal basis 1 but is not normative for Excel; both examples return 360, which does not distinguish the bases.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions supplies the period-0 stub interpretation, the zero-stub full-year fallback, and test-data organization. These are implementation references only; no source code is copied. Direct Excel checks are still needed for period indexing, period 0, fractional periods, leap dates, the zero-stub fallback, and undocumented invalid inputs.

derived_examples.basis: Actual/Actual day fraction 134/365 times cost 2400 and rate 0.15 because this interval contains no February 29; reference-derived, not a Microsoft-published result.
The NASD 30/360 stub is zero; the reference-derived evaluator profile falls back to cost*rate, capped at cost-salvage. Not a Microsoft-published result.

semantics.definition: Returns the number of unordered selections of number_chosen items from number distinct items, C(n,k).
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents truncation of numeric arguments, #VALUE! for nonnumeric arguments, #NUM! when either integer argument is negative or number is less than number_chosen, and COMBIN(8,2)=28.
semantics.truncation_and_domain_profile: Workbook Forge truncates arguments toward zero before checking the resulting integer domain. Microsoft documents truncation and domain constraints but does not specify their order for negative fractional values; direct Excel spot-checking is still needed.
semantics.implementation: The evaluator uses k = min(k, n-k), forms the exact integer coefficient with a bounded multiplicative recurrence, then rounds once to binary64; this avoids factorial intermediates and cross-runtime rounding drift.
semantics.coercion_profile: Workbook Forge applies its shared scalar numeric coercer: blank values, Boolean values, empty text, and ASCII numeric text are converted to numbers; nonnumeric text returns #VALUE! and existing formula errors propagate. Range rejection takes precedence, then the first existing formula error in argument order; if no formula error exists, scalar coercion proceeds left to right. Function-specific numeric-domain validation occurs after all scalar coercions succeed. For multi-argument combinatorics functions, a later invalid text argument returns #VALUE! before an earlier negative count produces #NUM!; this is an unverified Workbook Forge mixed-input profile. Microsoft does not specify these mixed-error precedence rules or subtype coercions.
semantics.range_behavior: MS-OE376 §3.17.2 lists the range-capable function arguments and does not list this function (FACTDOUBLE is listed). Normal formulas therefore use Office implicit intersection when possible; array-entered formulas receive full ranges. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array-entry context and returns #VALUE! for a range argument as a local scalar boundary, not as an Excel expected result.
semantics.numeric_profile: Workbook Forge uses finite binary64 scalar values and accepts integer arguments only through 2^53; larger magnitudes are rejected because adjacent integers are no longer all exactly representable. Within FACT, FACTDOUBLE, COMBIN, COMBINA, PERMUT, and PERMUTATIONA argument expressions, plain integer literals, unary signs, +, -, *, and nonnegative integer-power expressions preserve exact source integers through the boundary check, subject to a 65,536-bit intermediate cap. Exact integer division forms a ratio and rounds once to binary64; mixed or decimal operands use binary64 division. Decimal/scientific literals also follow binary64 parsing and may round before the check. The exact integer coefficient is rounded once to binary64 using round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. A result outside the finite binary64 range returns #NUM! as a local profile. Microsoft documents 15-digit worksheet precision and a largest formula result near 1.7976931348623158e+308, but does not specify the exact overflow error for this function. No direct Excel spot-check has been performed.

semantics.rate_period: rate is the rate per payment period and nper counts payments at that interval. Annual rates and payment periods must be converted to matching units, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.payment_timing: type=0 means end-of-period payments; type=1 means beginning-of-period payments.
semantics.cash_flow_sign: Payments made on the loan are negative in Microsoft's published examples; the evaluator preserves the PMT/IPMT/PPMT sign convention.
semantics.documented_constraints: Microsoft specifies #NUM! when rate<=0, nper<=0, pv<=0, start_period<1, end_period<1, start_period>end_period, or type is not 0 or 1.
semantics.period_aggregation: The requested range is inclusive. CUMIPMT aggregates IPMT components; CUMPRINC aggregates PPMT components.
semantics.equation_profile: Let L=log1p(rate) and D=-expm1(-nper*L). For end-timed periods first..last, let m=last-first+1 and z=(first-1-nper)*L+log_exprel(m*L)+log(L/rate), where log_exprel(x)=log(expm1(x)/x); then delta=-m*expm1(z) and CUMIPMT=-pv*rate*delta/D. For beginning timing, omit period 1 and divide the end-timed interest sum by 1+rate. The exact identity is CUMPRINC=selected_period_count*PMT(rate,nper,pv,0,type)-CUMIPMT, but the evaluator sums principal directly to avoid cancellation. Let L=log1p(rate) and D=1-exp(-nper*L). For an end-timed range ending at last with count selected periods, its principal log magnitude is log(pv)+(last-nper)*L+log1mexp(count*L)-log1mexp(nper*L), where log1mexp(x)=log(1-exp(-x)); negate the exponential of this value. For beginning timing, omit period 1 from that geometric principal range, divide it by 1+rate, and add the first PMT_due if selected. When nper*rate<1e-12, use the average-balance interest limit and zero-rate principal limit -pv*selected_period_count/nper. The range evaluation is O(1), with no period-by-period loop.
semantics.fractional_period_profile: Fractional start_period and end_period select the whole payment periods enclosed by the interval: ceil(start_period) through floor(end_period). A range containing no whole period returns zero. Microsoft does not specify fractional period behavior.
semantics.nper_profile: The evaluator follows the existing PMT model for fractional nper; Microsoft does not document fractional nper behavior for these functions.
semantics.end_period_profile: end_period greater than nper returns #NUM! in this evaluator, following the Apache reference range guard. Microsoft does not state this boundary on the function page.
semantics.numeric_coercion_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion: blanks and empty text become zero, booleans become 0/1, and ASCII numeric text is parsed. These coercions are evaluator profiles where Microsoft is silent.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. Invalid documented constraints return #NUM!; nonfinite inputs, nonfinite intermediates/results, and period endpoints above 2^53 also return #NUM! as evaluator limits. Microsoft does not define all error codes or precedence for these cases.
semantics.scalar_limits: Only scalar numeric arguments and results are supported. Ranges, arrays, locale-specific number parsing, Excel internal precision, and workbook-specific financial conventions are outside the evaluator profile.
semantics.excel_validation: The shared Python/Rust fixtures establish evaluator parity only. No direct Microsoft Excel spot-check has been performed.

semantics.equation_profile: Microsoft defines each amount as min((cost - prior depreciation)*factor/life, cost - salvage - prior depreciation). The evaluator uses the equivalent geometric book balance cost*(1-factor/life)^(period-1), then caps the amount at max(book-salvage,0). If factor/life>=1, period 1 consumes the depreciable basis and later periods return zero.
semantics.period_units: The period and life arguments use the same units. Microsoft examples cover daily, monthly, and yearly periods.
semantics.default_profile: Omitted factor defaults to 2, as Microsoft documents. An explicitly empty optional slot returns #VALUE! as an evaluator profile.

Cost>=salvage>=0, factor>0, life truncates to an integer >=1, and period truncates to 1..life. Microsoft says salvage may be zero but also states all five arguments must be positive; that wording conflicts with the zero-salvage example and optional factor. The chosen bounds, truncation, error, and exact-binary64 period limits are evaluator profiles.
semantics.calculation_profile: The requested period is calculated in constant time from the geometric book balance and is capped at the remaining depreciable basis. No loop over earlier periods is required. If factor/life underflows to zero in binary64, a logarithmic fallback preserves representable positive amounts; the associated book-value decay is below binary64 precision over the accepted period range.

semantics.definition: Returns the number rounded away from zero to the nearest even integer.
semantics.rounding: Take the ceiling of the absolute input; if that integer is odd, add one; restore the input sign. An existing even integer is unchanged. EVEN(0)=0 is derived from the documented rule.
semantics.input_coercion_profile: Uses the shared scalar numeric coercion: blank and empty text become 0, booleans become 0/1, and locale-independent ASCII numeric text is parsed. Microsoft does not specify these coercions on the EVEN page; this profile is not Excel-verified.
semantics.range_profile: The Microsoft Office formula specification says normal formulas apply implicit intersection to range arguments unless the function permits range arguments; EVEN is not listed as range-capable. Array-entered formulas use the full range and may return arrays. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array context, so it returns #VALUE! for ranges as a local scalar-limit profile, not an Excel result.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate before numeric evaluation.
semantics.numeric_precision_profile: The evaluator uses IEEE 754 binary64. semantics.definition: Returns the number of payment periods for an investment or loan with constant periodic payments and a constant rate.
semantics.equation_profile: For rate=0 and pmt!=0, nper=-(pv+fv)/pmt. Otherwise q=(pmt*(1+rate*type)-rate*fv)/(pmt*(1+rate*type)+rate*pv), and nper=ln(q)/ln(1+rate). The evaluator solves the analytic equation and does not round the result to a whole period.
semantics.rate_period: rate is the rate per payment period, and pmt is the constant payment for that same period. Microsoft documents that annual rate and payment periods must be converted to matching units.
semantics.payment_timing: type=0 or omitted means payments at each period end; type=1 means payments at each period beginning, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.cash_flow_sign: Cash paid out is negative and cash received is positive, consistent with Microsoft's periodic cash-flow guidance.
semantics.optional_slots: fv defaults to zero; type defaults to zero. The fv slot may be omitted while type is supplied in the following slot.
semantics.negative_and_fractional_results: The analytic result may be negative or fractional. Microsoft's published example returns -9.57859404; the evaluator preserves both signs and fractional periods.
semantics.calculation_profile: The evaluator normalizes cash flows before combining rate terms, uses log1p for the growth denominator and ratios near one, and uses a difference of logarithms for extreme positive ratios. This is a numerical stability choice, not a claim about Excel's internal algorithm or precision.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use the evaluator's shared numeric coercion: blank cells, empty text, and omitted optional slots become zero; FALSE/TRUE become 0/1; ASCII numeric text is parsed. These coercions are evaluator profiles where Microsoft does not specify them. After coercion, all inputs and the result must be finite, rate must be greater than -1, and type must be exactly 0 or 1.
semantics.zero_rate_profile: At rate=0, NPER returns the linear solution -(pv+fv)/pmt when pmt is nonzero. A zero payment, all-zero cash flows, a zero logarithm term, a negative logarithm ratio, or a non-unique solution returns #NUM! as an evaluator profile; Microsoft does not specify these error boundaries. A zero payment can still return a finite result when the nonzero-rate logarithm ratio is valid.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: Argument calculation errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. Numeric validation checks finite inputs, then rate, then type, then the zero-rate or logarithm solution domain; Microsoft does not specify this precedence.
semantics.scalar_limits: Only scalar numeric results are supported. Arrays, locale-dependent numeric text, workbook-specific currency semantics, and Excel-specific internal precision are outside this evaluator profile.
semantics.microsoft_example_note: The published example omitting type has an argument table that implies type=0, but its prose says beginning-of-period payments. The shared fixture follows the formula and result column and preserves the wording discrepancy for review.

semantics.definition: Returns the number rounded away from zero to the nearest odd integer.
semantics.rounding: Take the ceiling of the absolute input; if that integer is even, add one; restore the input sign. An existing odd integer is unchanged. ODD(0)=1 is derived from the documented rule.
semantics.input_coercion_profile: Uses the shared scalar numeric coercion: blank and empty text become 0, booleans become 0/1, and locale-independent ASCII numeric text is parsed. Microsoft does not specify these coercions on the ODD page; this profile is not Excel-verified.
semantics.range_profile: The Microsoft Office formula specification says normal formulas apply implicit intersection to range arguments unless the function permits range arguments; ODD is not listed as range-capable. Array-entered formulas use the full range and may return arrays. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array context, so it returns #VALUE! for ranges as a local scalar-limit profile, not an Excel result.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate before numeric evaluation.
semantics.numeric_precision_profile: For finite binary64 input with absolute value at least 2^53, the evaluator returns #NUM! because the next odd integer cannot be represented exactly. This is a Workbook Forge numeric boundary, not a Microsoft-documented error. Microsoft also documents worksheet number precision as 15 digits, so 16-digit literals in the boundary fixtures are local engine probes rather than Excel oracles.
semantics.excel_validation: No direct Microsoft Excel spot-check has been performed.

semantics.definition: Returns the number of ordered selections of number_chosen objects from number distinct objects without repetition: nPr = n × (n−1) × … for the selected count.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents two required arguments, truncation of both arguments, #VALUE! for nonnumeric arguments, #NUM! when number ≤ 0, number_chosen < 0, or number < number_chosen, PERMUT(3,2)=6, and PERMUT(100,3)=970200.
semantics.truncation_and_domain_profile: Workbook Forge truncates arguments toward zero before checking the resulting integer domain. Microsoft documents truncation and domain constraints but does not specify their order for negative fractions; direct Excel spot-checking remains outstanding.
semantics.implementation: Python and Rust independently form the falling product directly, without factorial division. The exact integer product is rounded once to binary64; early bounds avoid unbounded work when overflow is guaranteed.
semantics.coercion_profile: Workbook Forge applies its shared scalar numeric coercer: blank values, Boolean values, empty text, and ASCII numeric text are converted to numbers; nonnumeric text returns #VALUE! and existing formula errors propagate. Range rejection takes precedence, then the first existing formula error in argument order; if no formula error exists, scalar coercion proceeds left to right. Function-specific numeric-domain validation occurs after all scalar coercions succeed. For multi-argument combinatorics functions, a later invalid text argument returns #VALUE! before an earlier negative count produces #NUM!; this is an unverified Workbook Forge mixed-input profile. Microsoft does not specify these mixed-error precedence rules or subtype coercions.
semantics.range_behavior: The Office range-capability list does not include this function. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array-entry context and returns #VALUE! for range arguments as a local scalar boundary; that output is not asserted as an Excel result.
semantics.numeric_profile: Workbook Forge accepts finite binary64 scalar values and integer arguments only through 2^53. Within FACT, FACTDOUBLE, COMBIN, COMBINA, PERMUT, and PERMUTATIONA argument expressions, plain integer literals, unary signs, +, -, *, and nonnegative integer-power expressions preserve exact source integers through the boundary check, subject to a 65,536-bit intermediate cap. Exact integer division forms a ratio and rounds once to binary64; mixed or decimal operands use binary64 division. Decimal/scientific literals also follow binary64 parsing and may round before the check. The local result profile accepts integer arguments through 2^53 and returns #NUM! if the exact positive product rounds outside finite binary64. Choosing zero returns 1; when a valid selection count exceeds 170, overflow is guaranteed because nPr ≥ r!. Microsoft does not specify result rounding or a function-specific overflow code. Coercion, negative-fraction order, and overflow have not been spot-checked in Excel.

semantics.definition: Calculates the constant periodic payment for a loan or investment at a constant rate; it includes principal and interest but not taxes, reserves, or fees.
semantics.equation_profile: For rate != 0, PMT = -(pv + fv/(1+rate)^nper) / ((1+rate*type)*(1-(1+rate)^(-nper))/rate); for rate = 0, PMT = -(pv+fv)/nper. The stable evaluator uses equivalent log1p/expm1 expressions.
semantics.optional_slots: fv defaults to zero. type defaults to zero.
semantics.rate_period: rate is the interest rate per payment period; nper counts payment periods using the same interval. Annual rates must be converted to the payment interval, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.payment_timing: type=0 or omitted means payments at each period end; type=1 means payments at each period beginning, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.cash_flow_sign: Cash paid out is negative and cash received is positive, as Microsoft documents for annuity functions.
semantics.calculation_profile: The evaluator uses log1p/expm1-based periodic growth and annuity factors, with an exact zero-rate limit. Excel's internal numeric algorithm and precision are not specified by the cited pages.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use the evaluator's shared numeric coercion before domain checks: blank cells, empty text, and omitted optional slots become zero; FALSE/TRUE become 0/1; and ASCII numeric text is parsed. Microsoft does not specify all of these coercions, so they are evaluator profiles. After coercion, this evaluator requires finite inputs and results, rejects rate <= -1 and negative nper with #NUM!, requires type to equal 0 or 1, evaluates fractional nper through the analytic equation, and returns #DIV/0! for PMT when the annuity factor is zero.
semantics.zero_period_profile: At nper=0, FV returns the negated present value and PV returns the negated future value; PMT returns #DIV/0! because its annuity factor is zero. Microsoft does not specify zero-period outcomes on the cited pages.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: Argument calculation errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. When more than one numeric profile boundary is violated, argument order and then rate, nper, type validation determine the returned evaluator error; Microsoft does not specify this precedence.
semantics.scalar_limits: Only scalar numeric results are supported. Arrays, locale-dependent numeric text, workbook-specific currency or date semantics, and Excel-specific internal precision are outside this evaluator profile.

semantics.definition: Returns the payment on principal for a given period for an investment with periodic constant payments and a constant interest rate.
semantics.equation_profile: PPMT(rate,per,nper,pv,fv,type)=PMT(rate,nper,pv,fv,type)-IPMT(rate,per,nper,pv,fv,type). This shares payment timing and sign conventions with PMT and IPMT.
semantics.rate_period: rate is the interest rate per payment period; nper counts payment periods using the same interval. Annual rates must be converted to the payment interval, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.payment_timing: type=0 or omitted means payments at each period end; type=1 means payments at each period beginning, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.cash_flow_sign: Cash paid out is negative and cash received is positive, consistent with Microsoft’s periodic cash-flow guidance.
semantics.optional_slots: fv defaults to zero and type defaults to zero. An omitted fv slot is retained when a following type argument is supplied.
semantics.calculation_profile: The evaluator obtains the payment from the existing PMT engine and computes prior-period growth with log1p/expm1-based expressions. This is a numerical stability and code-reuse choice, not a claim about Excel’s internal algorithm or precision.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use the evaluator’s shared scalar number coercion: blank cells, empty text, and omitted optional slots become zero; FALSE/TRUE become 0/1; and ASCII numeric text is parsed. Microsoft does not specify all these coercions. Inputs and results must be finite, rate must be greater than -1, type must equal 0 or 1, and per must be between 1 and nper. Fractional per and nper values inside those bounds are evaluated analytically as an evaluator profile.
semantics.zero_rate_profile: At rate=0, IPMT returns zero and PPMT returns PMT. For a nonzero rate, type=1 and per=1 also gives zero interest; later beginning-of-period interest adjusts the end-of-period component by 1+rate. These numerical boundaries are evaluator profiles pending Excel spot-checks.
semantics.error_profile: Invalid type, a rate at or below -1, an out-of-range period, nonfinite inputs, and nonfinite results return #NUM! in this evaluator profile. Argument calculation errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. Microsoft documents the period and type constraints but does not specify exact errors or precedence for these invalid cases.
semantics.component_identity: For each supported input, PPMT = PMT(rate,nper,pv,fv,type) - IPMT, so IPMT + PPMT equals the periodic PMT up to floating-point rounding.
semantics.scalar_limits: Only scalar numeric results are supported. Arrays, locale-dependent numeric text, workbook-specific currency semantics, and Excel-specific internal precision are outside this evaluator profile.

semantics.definition: Generates a rectangular array of sequential numbers.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents SEQUENCE(rows,[columns],[start],[step]), says optional arguments default to 1, describes rows and columns, and states that a final array result spills into the worksheet grid.
semantics.implementation: Python and Rust independently construct the same row-major rectangular array. ArrayValue preserves shape and the public evaluate_result API returns it. IF, IFERROR, IFNA, IFS, and SWITCH preserve a selected array result. SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, MIN, MAX, AND, OR, CONCAT, TEXTJOIN, and COUNTBLANK consume generated arrays through their existing flattening rules. Binary arithmetic (+, -, *, /, ^), comparisons, and concatenation also lift elementwise across equal-shaped ranges/arrays and broadcast scalar operands.
semantics.omission_profile: The engines allow omitted rows when a later argument is present and default the omitted row dimension to 1. Microsoft says an omitted rows argument requires another argument but does not show its resulting shape; this Workbook Forge choice is unverified.
semantics.dimension_profile: Both engines use the shared scalar numeric coercer, truncate dimensions toward zero, and return #NUM! for zero or negative dimensions. Microsoft’s SEQUENCE page does not specify these coercions or error codes; they are Workbook Forge profiles.
semantics.allocation_profile: Both engines reject arrays larger than 100000 cells before allocation. The cap reuses the existing evaluator range budget and is a Workbook Forge resource policy; Microsoft worksheet and array limits are larger and context-dependent.
semantics.numeric_profile: Start and step use finite binary64 values. Values follow start + row-major-index × step. Nonfinite inputs or generated outputs return #NUM! under a local Workbook Forge profile.
semantics.worksheet_boundary: ArrayValue is a computed result, not a spill projection. Workbook Forge does not place spill cells, detect blocked/merged/table destinations, model A1# or @ implicit intersection, or calculate dependency invalidation for spill regions.
semantics.compatibility_limit: Shared fixtures establish Python/Rust parity for this bounded evaluator profile; no direct Excel spot-checks have been performed.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: Arguments are evaluated left to right; the first encountered formula error or evaluation failure stops later arguments. Ordinary scalar coercion follows expression evaluation, so a later formula error can precede coercion of an earlier nonnumeric text value. A non-finite numeric literal fails when encountered. These mixed-error ordering choices are Workbook Forge profiles, not Microsoft claims.
semantics.array_operator_boundary_profile: Workbook Forge lifts binary arithmetic (+, -, *, /, ^), comparisons, and concatenation elementwise over bounded ranges and arrays. Two array operands must have exactly equal shapes; scalar operands broadcast on either side. Shape mismatches return #VALUE!, and cell-level formula errors remain in their result cells. For binary comparisons, numeric-like operands are checked before type dispatch; finite values use binary64 precision, and nonfinite/out-of-range values return #NUM!; ASCII text is case-insensitive, while text comparison is exact if either operand contains non-ASCII characters; worksheet numbers, text and Booleans have distinct ranks in that order; blank adapts to the other operand type (zero, empty text or FALSE). Numeric text is not parsed for comparison, and no Boolean-to-number equality coercion occurs. Type ranking and blank rules remain an Excel-targeted unobserved profile; native primitives retain their separate legacy comparison contract. Binary operand errors propagate left to right: a left formula error precedes a non-finite right operand, while a non-finite left numeric operand returns #NUM! before a right formula error. This error precedence is a local Workbook Forge profile. These comparison precision, collation, and coercion rules are local Workbook Forge profiles; values beyond Excel's documented 15-digit precision are not Excel oracles. Unary operators, array constants, general broadcasting, and worksheet spill projection are not modeled. Microsoft documents elementwise array operators; this narrower shape and error profile is not a claim of complete Excel semantics.

semantics.definition: Returns straight-line depreciation of an asset for one period.
semantics.equation_profile: SLN=(cost-salvage)/life. The amount depreciated is spread evenly across each life period.
semantics.period_units: life is the number of periods over which the asset is depreciated. Microsoft does not prescribe calendar units; each unit is one depreciation period.
semantics.signed_basis_profile: The evaluator permits salvage greater than cost and returns signed depreciation. Microsoft does not state a salvage-versus-cost restriction on the Excel function page.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion: blanks and empty text become zero, booleans become 0/1, and ASCII numeric text is parsed. The evaluator requires cost>=0, salvage>=0, and life>0, following the explicit validator pattern in the Apache-2.0 reference; Microsoft does not specify these bounds, fractional life behavior, or coercions for Excel SLN. Fractional positive life values are evaluated directly.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate. Negative cost or salvage, nonpositive life, nonfinite inputs, or a nonfinite result return #NUM! as evaluator profiles. Microsoft does not specify error codes or precedence for these cases.
semantics.calculation_profile: A scalar arithmetic kernel is kept separate from domain validation. The shared Python/Rust fixtures establish the evaluator profile only; they are not direct Excel results except for the cited Microsoft example.
semantics.excel_validation: No direct Microsoft Excel spot-check has been performed.
semantics.scalar_limits: Arrays, ranges, locale-dependent numeric parsing, workbook-specific asset-accounting conventions, and Excel internal precision are outside this evaluator profile.

semantics.definition: Returns the rows or columns of an array in sorted order.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents the array input, optional sort_index, ascending 1 or descending -1 sort_order, and by_col selection. Defaults are index 1, ascending, and row-wise sorting. The output has the same shape as the source and spills when it is the final worksheet formula.
semantics.implementation: Independent Python and Rust kernels accept ranges or bounded ArrayValue inputs and return a same-shape ArrayValue. Sorting uses source indices and a stable sort, preserving record order for ties and carrying non-key cells with their records.
semantics.selector_profile: Workbook Forge accepts finite integral numeric sort_index and sort_order selectors and a Boolean by_col selector. The selected index must be within the source axis; order must be 1 or -1. Invalid selectors return #VALUE!.
semantics.comparison_profile: The selected key axis must contain one homogeneous type: finite binary64 numbers or text. Numeric keys compare as binary64. Text keys lowercase ASCII letters consistently and keep non-ASCII characters exact. Mixed types, blanks, and Booleans return #VALUE!; non-finite numeric keys return #NUM!. Selected-key errors propagate before type validation. Validation then follows key-axis order. Numeric values in returned records are normalized to finite binary64 values; non-finite output numbers return #NUM!. These are Workbook Forge profiles, not claims about Excel collation or coercion.
semantics.allocation_profile: Source ranges and ArrayValue inputs are bounded to 100000 cells before materialization; a larger referenced range returns #NUM! under the Workbook Forge range limit. SORT output cannot exceed source dimensions.
semantics.worksheet_boundary: The evaluator returns the sorted formula value and shape; it does not place spill cells, detect blockers, model A1# references, or calculate spill dependencies.
semantics.compatibility_limit: Shared fixtures and direct API tests establish Python/Rust agreement for this bounded profile. Microsoft documents the function and its selectors, but comparison and coercion details remain local profiles. No direct Excel Desktop spot-checks have been performed.

semantics.definition: Returns sum-of-years-digits depreciation of an asset for a specified period.
semantics.equation_profile: SYD=(cost-salvage)*2*(life-per+1)/(life*(life+1)). The weights decrease linearly from life through 1 and their sum is life*(life+1)/2. The implementation evaluates the equivalent bounded weight 2*((life-per+1)/(life+1)) and multiplies it by (cost-salvage)/life, avoiding an oversized triangular denominator and avoiding division by a tiny life before the basis is scaled.
semantics.period_units: per must use the same units as life, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.schedule_identity: For integer life L, the sum of SYD over periods 1..L equals cost-salvage. This identity grounds the derived full-schedule fixtures.
semantics.signed_basis_profile: The evaluator permits salvage greater than cost and returns signed depreciation. Microsoft does not state a salvage-versus-cost restriction on the Excel function page.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion: blanks and empty text become zero, booleans become 0/1, and ASCII numeric text is parsed. The evaluator requires cost>=0, salvage>=0, life>0, and 0<per<=life, following the explicit validator pattern in the Apache-2.0 reference; Microsoft does not specify these bounds or coercions for Excel SYD. Fractional life/per inputs satisfying this interval are retained and evaluated analytically, consistent with the reference test pattern but not checked in Excel.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate. Negative cost or salvage, nonpositive life, per outside (0,life], nonfinite inputs, or a nonfinite result return #NUM! as evaluator profiles. Microsoft does not specify exact errors or precedence for these cases.
semantics.calculation_profile: The evaluator separates argument validation from the scalar depreciation kernel. Its weighted schedule is constant-time and does not loop over earlier periods.

semantics.scalar_limits: Arrays, ranges, locale-dependent numeric parsing, workbook-specific asset-accounting conventions, and Excel internal precision are outside this evaluator profile.

semantics.definition: Returns depreciation over a requested interval using declining balance, with optional switching to straight-line depreciation.
semantics.equation_profile: Microsoft describes VDB as using the double-declining-balance method or another factor. Its DDB page defines each declining-balance amount as min(book_before_period*factor/life, book_before_period-salvage). The evaluator compares that amount with straight-line depreciation over the remaining life and switches at the first whole period where straight-line is greater, unless no_switch is TRUE.
semantics.interval_profile: Evaluator profile: each unit period contributes its period depreciation multiplied by the overlap length with [start_period,end_period). Fractional endpoints are prorated; the interval is evaluated directly rather than by subtracting two large cumulative totals. This profile is not asserted to match Excel for general fractional starts.
semantics.fractional_life_profile: Fractional life is accepted as an evaluator profile. The final sub-period uses the remaining fractional duration; with switching enabled the remaining basis is allocated over that tail when straight-line exceeds the capped DDB amount.
semantics.default_profile: Microsoft documents factor default 2 and says no_switch FALSE or omitted permits switching; TRUE prevents the switch. An explicitly omitted optional factor defaults to 2 even when no_switch is supplied. A blank referenced factor coerces to zero and is rejected; a blank referenced no_switch value is false as an evaluator profile.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion for cost, salvage, life, interval endpoints, and factor. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<=cost, life and factor must be positive, and 0<=start_period<=end_period<=life. Life is limited to 9,007,199,254,740,991 periods so whole-period arithmetic remains exact in binary64. no_switch uses the evaluator logical coercion profile: Booleans and numeric values use shared truth coercion: zero, blank, and empty text are false, any nonzero number is true, and nonempty text is rejected. These bounds and coercions are evaluator profiles; Microsoft does not fully specify them.
semantics.calculation_profile: The no-switch DDB schedule is summed as a geometric series with an explicit salvage-cap period. The switch period is found by binary search over whole periods, then the remaining straight-line interval is calculated directly. Work is O(log life), not proportional to the number of periods. Python and Rust use independent implementations. If factor/life underflows to zero, a log-space fallback preserves representable depreciation amounts.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. Invalid bounds, nonfinite inputs/results, and life above the exact-period limit return #NUM!; missing required arguments and invalid logical text return #VALUE!. Microsoft does not specify all error codes or precedence.
semantics.documented_conflicts: Microsoft says salvage may be 0 and publishes examples whose start_period is 0, but the same page says all arguments except no_switch must be positive. The evaluator accepts zero salvage and zero start_period based on the explicit examples and statement.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions reports that Excel may return a different total for a fractional interval than for adjacent split intervals when straight-line switching is enabled. Its own implementation remains additive; this evaluator likewise defines a deterministic prorated schedule. No split-interval additivity is claimed for Excel, and the discrepancy needs a direct Excel spot-check.

Text, logical values and an empty cell reached that way are ignored, as they are for the same cell named directly, so with A1 = TRUE or A1 empty AVERAGE(IF(TRUE,A1),10) is 10, and a zero in A1 is counted. Microsoft's AVERAGE page says "If a range or cell reference argument contains text, logical values, or empty cells, those values are ignored; however, cells with the value zero are included." A value typed directly and selected the same way is still a typed value under the provisional policy in direct_policy_conflict, so AVERAGE(IF(TRUE,TRUE),10) is 5.5. No Microsoft sentence says what AVERAGE does with a one-cell reference selected by IF or the other functions. Treating it as a reference is a Workbook Forge profile, the same rule this evaluator already applied to COUNT, AND and OR, and it has not been checked in Excel. IFERROR still returns empty text, a typed value, when the selected cell is empty, so AVERAGE(IFERROR(A1,0),10) with A1 empty is #VALUE! by text_profile. IFNA keeps a selected empty cell as an empty reference in both evaluators, although Microsoft's IFNA page says "If value or value_if_na is an empty cell, IFNA treats it as an empty string value ("")." AVERAGE(IFNA(A1,0),10) with A1 empty is therefore 10, and no fixture pins that value. INDEX is a reference here only when its first argument is a range. The Rust evaluator's INDEX also accepts a typed value or one cell as its first argument, and directly inside AVERAGE that result is read as it was before this profile, so AVERAGE(INDEX(TRUE,1),10) is 5.5 there; the Python evaluator's INDEX returns #VALUE! for it. semantics.definition: Searches the first row of a table for a value and returns the value in the same column from the row given by row_index_num.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents that first-row values can be text, numbers, or logical values; uppercase and lowercase text are equivalent; a row_index_num less than 1 returns #VALUE! and one greater than the number of rows returns #REF!; range_lookup TRUE or omitted returns an approximate match, the largest value less than lookup_value when no exact match exists, and requires the first row in ascending order (numbers, then text, then FALSE, then TRUE); a lookup_value smaller than the smallest first-row value returns #N/A; range_lookup FALSE finds an exact match or returns #N/A, and a text lookup_value may then use the wildcards ? and * with ~ as the escape. Examples over the Axles, Bearings, Bolts table: HLOOKUP("Axles",A1:C4,2,TRUE)=4, HLOOKUP("Bearings",A1:C4,3,FALSE)=7, HLOOKUP("B",A1:C4,3,TRUE)=5, HLOOKUP("Bolts",A1:C4,4)=11.
semantics.table_profile: table_array is a range, a computed array, or a single-cell reference, which is a table of one row and one column. A value typed directly is not a table and returns #VALUE!. Array constants are not supported by the formula parser, so Microsoft's array-constant example cannot be entered.
semantics.comparison_profile: Only first-row values of the same type as lookup_value are compared: numbers with numbers by value, text with text after per-character Unicode lowercasing and then by code point, logical values with FALSE before TRUE. Microsoft does not specify comparison across types, the text collation, or these empty and error cases; they are unverified Workbook Forge profiles, and Excel's text order may differ from code point order outside ASCII letters and digits.
semantics.exact_profile: An exact lookup returns the leftmost match. A text lookup_value containing ?, * or ~ is a wildcard pattern matched against text values only, within the evaluator's shared wildcard work limit.
semantics.approximate_profile: An approximate lookup uses the largest first-row value that is not above lookup_value, and the rightmost one when several are equal. The result does not depend on the row being sorted; Microsoft says an unsorted row may give an incorrect value in Excel, so results on unsorted rows are not asserted as Excel results. Wildcards are ordinary characters in an approximate lookup.
semantics.argument_profile: Arguments are read in order and the first problem is returned: lookup_value (an error value is returned; a range or array returns #VALUE!), then table_array, then row_index_num (shared scalar numeric coercer, truncated toward zero, then the documented bounds), then range_lookup (shared logical conversion: a number is TRUE unless zero, an empty cell or empty text is FALSE, other text returns #VALUE!). An explicitly empty argument returns #VALUE!. Microsoft does not specify this precedence.
semantics.result_profile: The returned cell value is passed through unchanged: an error value there is the result, and an empty cell gives an empty result.
semantics.compatibility_limit: No behaviour of this function has been spot-checked in Excel.

semantics.definition: Returns the net present value of a series of cash flows one period apart, the first one period from now, at a discount rate per period.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents a required rate and 1 to 254 value arguments that are equally spaced in time and occur at the end of each period; the order of the values is the order of the cash flows; the investment begins one period before the value1 cash flow, so a cash flow at the start of the first period is added to the result rather than included in the values; in an array or reference only numbers are counted and empty cells, logical values, text, or error values are ignored. semantics.equation: NPV is the sum over i = 1..n of value_i / (1 + rate)^i. Microsoft's page shows the formula as an image; its three examples reproduce under this equation.
semantics.value_profile: values is read by the aggregate rule. Typed directly, a number, a logical value (TRUE is 1, FALSE is 0), or text holding a plain decimal number counts and other text returns #VALUE!. Inside a cell reference, range, or computed array only numbers count; text, logical values, and empty cells are ignored and do not take a period, while a zero is a cash flow. A single value is a one-entry series. Array constants are not supported by the formula parser. Microsoft's sentence on directly typed values reads: "Arguments that are empty cells, logical values, or text representations of numbers, error values, or text that cannot be translated into numbers are ignored." It is not clear enough to implement, and Workbook Forge departs from it as written in three ways: NPV(1,TRUE,"4") counts the logical value and the numeric text and is 1.5, NPV(1,"abc") is #VALUE!, and an error value typed directly, as in NPV(1,#N/A), is returned. These are unverified Workbook Forge profiles shared with the other aggregates.
semantics.error_profile: An error value anywhere in the arguments, including inside a reference or array, is returned; the first one in reading order wins. This is an unverified Workbook Forge profile. Microsoft's page says error values in an array or reference are ignored; Workbook Forge returns them so that a broken input never yields a number.
semantics.rate_profile: A rate or guess argument is a single value converted with the shared scalar numeric coercer: blank values, logical values, empty text, and ASCII numeric text convert to numbers and other text returns #VALUE!. A range or array there returns #VALUE! as a local scalar boundary. An explicitly empty argument and an argument count outside the documented syntax return #VALUE!. These are unverified Workbook Forge profiles. A rate of -100 percent returns #DIV/0! because every discount factor is zero; this is checked after the values are read. A rate below -100 percent is evaluated with the equation as written. Microsoft documents neither case.
semantics.empty_profile: When no number is counted the result is 0. Microsoft does not document this case.
semantics.implementation: The discount factor is built by repeated multiplication by 1 + rate, and the quotients are added in cash-flow order with a binary64 left fold. A discount factor that underflows to zero returns #NUM!.
semantics.order_profile: Arguments are read one at a time from left to right, each one completely, and the first problem met is returned: a wrong argument count first, then for each argument in turn its error value or its value that cannot be read. The function's own checks follow in the order this specification lists them. Microsoft does not specify precedence among several problems; this is an unverified Workbook Forge profile.
semantics.numeric_profile: Inputs and results are finite binary64 numbers. A result that is not finite returns #NUM!, and a zero result carries no sign. Microsoft does not specify a function-specific overflow code; this profile has not been spot-checked in Excel.
semantics.compatibility_limit: No behaviour of this function has been spot-checked in Excel.

semantics.definition: Returns the internal rate of return of a series of cash flows one period apart: the rate at which their net present value, with the first flow undiscounted, is zero.

semantics.iteration_profile: Microsoft says only that Excel uses an iterative technique; the technique here is a Workbook Forge profile and Excel's internal method is not known. After 20 tries without such a step the result is #NUM!. A guess at or below -100 percent, a value or slope that is not finite, and a zero slope also return #NUM!. semantics.definition: Returns the net present value of cash flows on given dates, discounted to the first date on a 365-day year.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents that the first payment corresponds to a cost or payment at the beginning of the investment and later payments are discounted on a 365-day year; the values must contain at least one positive and one negative value; the first date begins the schedule and all other dates must be later but may occur in any order; numbers in dates are truncated to integers; a nonnumeric argument returns #VALUE!; a number in dates that is not a valid date returns #VALUE!; a date that precedes the starting date returns #NUM!; a different number of values and dates returns #NUM!. Example: XNPV(.09,A2:A6,B2:B6) for -10000, 2750, 4250, 3250, 2750 on 1/1/2008, 3/1/2008, 10/30/2008, 2/15/2009, 4/1/2009 is $2,086.65; January 1, 2008 is serial number 39448.
semantics.equation: XNPV is the sum over i of P_i / (1 + rate)^((d_i - d_1) / 365). Microsoft's page shows the formula as an image; its example reproduces under this equation.
semantics.schedule_profile: values and dates are each a range, a computed array, or a single value, read row by row and paired in reading order. Every entry must be a number: text (including a date held as text), a logical value, or an empty cell returns #VALUE! and is neither skipped nor read as zero. Microsoft documents #VALUE! for a nonnumeric argument on the XNPV page; treating logical values and empty cells as nonnumeric is a Workbook Forge profile. Dates are truncated toward zero to whole days. A date outside serial numbers 0 through 2,958,465 (December 31, 9999) returns #VALUE!. A different number of values and dates returns #NUM!, and so does a date before the first date. Every date is validated before the counts are compared, and the counts before the date order; Microsoft does not specify that order. Time is counted in 365-day years from the first date. Serial numbers are used as given; the workbook's 1900 or 1904 date system does not change differences between dates.

Its remarks name an error only for a date that precedes the first date. Workbook Forge accepts a later payment dated on the first date and gives it exponent 0, so it is not discounted; refusing it would need an error that Microsoft does not name. This departs from the sentence as written and is an unverified Workbook Forge profile.

semantics.definition: Returns the interest rate per period of an annuity.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents that RATE is calculated by iteration and can have zero or more solutions; if the successive results do not converge to within 0.0000001 after 20 iterations, RATE returns #NUM!; fv omitted is 0; type is 0 or omitted for payments at the end of the period and 1 for the beginning; guess omitted is 10 percent; if pmt is omitted, fv must be included. Examples for 4 years, a payment of -200, and a loan of 8000: RATE(A2*12,A3,A4) is 1% and RATE(A2*12,A3,A4)*12 is 9.24%.
semantics.equation: RATE is a rate r above -100 percent that satisfies the annuity equation on Microsoft's PV page: pv*(1+r)^nper + pmt*(1+r*type)*((1+r)^nper - 1)/r + fv = 0, and pmt*nper + pv + fv = 0 at a zero rate.

Workbook Forge uses Newton's method on the rate with the analytic slope of the equation, starting from guess. A try computes one Newton step. A step that would put the rate at or below -100 percent moves the rate halfway to -100 percent instead and still counts as a try. The result is the rate after a Newton step that moved it by no more than 0.0000001, which is how the documented accuracy is applied. After 20 tries without such a step the result is #NUM!. A guess at or below -100 percent, a value or slope that is not finite, and a zero slope also return #NUM!. Where the equation has several roots, or the search does not settle, Excel may return a different root or a number where Workbook Forge returns #NUM!, and the reverse; only results on which both converge to the same root are expected to agree, and then only within the documented accuracy. At a rate of exactly zero a try uses the limit of the equation and of its slope. The annuity equation can also hold at -100 percent itself, for example when every payment is made at the start of the period and fv is 0; that is not a rate above -100 percent. A search that settles within 0.0000001 of -100 percent therefore returns #NUM!, and so does a genuine rate that close to the boundary.

An explicitly empty fv or type counts as 0, as in PMT, and so does an explicitly empty pmt when fv is given. Any other explicitly empty argument, including guess, returns #VALUE!. semantics.domain_profile: After conversion nper must be greater than 0 and type must be 0 or 1; otherwise the result is #NUM!. A fractional nper is evaluated with the equation. Microsoft does not name these errors.

Microsoft's page shows the formula as an image; its three examples reproduce under this equation.

Fractional powers use the platform's binary64 power function, which can differ in the last digit between the Python engine, the native Rust engine, and the WebAssembly build.

semantics.numeric_profile: Inputs and results are finite binary64 numbers. A result that is not finite returns #NUM!, and a zero result carries no sign. Microsoft does not specify a function-specific overflow code; this profile has not been spot-checked in Excel.
semantics.compatibility_limit: No behaviour of this function has been spot-checked in Excel.
